prerequisiteBridge: Represent one population recording as a vector. If N neurons are recorded simultaneously, their firing rates at one moment form an N-dimensional vector r. Each plotted point is not a neuron; it is the state of the entire population at that moment. PCA or a factor model describes those points with K coordinates, where K is smaller than N. Low dimensionality does not mean that only a few neurons were recorded; it means that the variation of many neurons is constrained by a few shared variables.

Interpret the linear map \(C\alpha +d\) as a multidimensional shadow. \(\alpha\) is a K-dimensional latent coordinate, each column of C specifies the activity pattern that one latent factor leaves across N neurons, and d is the mean offset. The shapes must be C: N×K, \(\alpha\): K×1, and output: N×1. Adding \(\Sigma\) acknowledges trial noise and unmodeled fluctuations even for the same latent state.

A Gaussian process does not mean that activity has a Gaussian-shaped profile. It assigns a joint distribution to a time-varying latent function at every pair of times. The kernel \(K(t,t')\) sets how long separated points remain similar. In a squared-exponential kernel, \(\tau\) is the smoothing time scale; larger \(\tau\) makes the latent trajectory vary more slowly. This distinction lets us discuss smooth trajectories, preparatory states, linear readouts, and closed-loop decoders separately.

modules.title: Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories
paragraphs: A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded.

Stack all neuronal rates at one moment into \(r(t)\), so each reach condition traces an N-dimensional trajectory. If most variance lies on a few PCs, the trajectory is close to a low-dimensional subspace. A single-neuron curve is the shadow of the high-dimensional trajectory on one coordinate axis. Multiple phase-shifted shadows can arise from one rotating or curved population trajectory, so tuning and dynamics are compatible observations.

PCA orders dimensions by variance; it does not know which dimension drives muscles. A low-variance dimension may carry a small but behaviorally crucial output, especially if the readout has high gain along it. Conversely, a large-variance dimension may be output-null preparation. Judging usefulness requires both neural covariance and the behavioral readout, not explained variance alone.

The two-dimensional loops or clusters in teaching figures are projections. Overlap may result from truncation, while separation may be exaggerated by normalization. Record the time axis, condition colors, whether trials were averaged, and whether PCs were fitted jointly across conditions. If PCA is fitted separately per condition, the trajectories no longer share coordinates and cannot be compared for target-specific preparation.
keyPoints: Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code.
Single-cell tuning can be a coordinate projection of a low-dimensional population trajectory.
PCA variance and motor potency are different criteria.

derivation.title: Directional tuning as a linear projection of a two-dimensional movement vector
derivation.setup: Write a two-dimensional reach direction as a unit vector and let the neuron respond linearly to its two coordinates.

steps.title: Write the direction vector
steps.explanation: The unit movement vector at angle \(\theta\) has horizontal and vertical components.

steps.title: Write the sensitivity direction
steps.explanation: Express preferred direction as a unit vector too, with modulation gain k.

steps.title: Compute the dot product
steps.explanation: Apply the cosine angle-difference identity to obtain the tuning curve.

symbolNotes: r and b are in Hz; k is a modulation amplitude in Hz.
\(\theta\) and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) must use the same angular unit and are conventionally treated as radians inside trigonometric functions.
derivation.unitsCheck: The direction vectors in the dot product are dimensionless; multiplying by k yields Hz, which can be added to baseline b.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(k=0\), every direction gives b. At \(\theta =\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) the rate is b+k, and in the opposite direction it is b-k.

workedExample.title: Compute tuning at four directions
workedExample.problem: A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\).
steps: At \(\pi /2\) and \(3\pi /2\), the cosine is 0, giving 20 Hz in both cases.
workedExample.result: The four rates are 28, 20, 12, and 20 Hz, respectively.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The maximum and minimum are symmetric around the 20 Hz baseline, and their mean remains 20 Hz.

pitfalls: Treating a cosine-fit preferred direction as an immutable causal label.
Mistaking the smoothness of a trial-averaged projection for noise-free single trials.

modules.title: Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model
paragraphs: Let \(r_{t}\) be the observed vector from N neurons in time bin t and \(\alpha _{t}\) contain K latent factors. Conditional on \(\alpha _{t}\), \(r_{t}\) follows a multivariate Gaussian with \(\operatorname{mean} C\alpha _{t}+d\) and covariance \(\Sigma\). Rows of C correspond to neurons, columns to factors, and d is each neuron's baseline. For spike counts, the Gaussian is an approximation; with very narrow bins or low rates, a Poisson observation model may be more appropriate.

A K-dimensional trajectory in latent space is embedded by C into N-dimensional activity space. The column span of C is the shared-activity subspace allowed by the model, while \(\Sigma\) usually absorbs neuron-specific residuals. Shared variation does not require neuron pairs to have identical waveforms: positive and negative loadings allow one factor to produce different amplitudes and directions across cells.

The conditional observation mean has a coordinate reparameterization. For any invertible K×K matrix A, define \(\alpha '=A\alpha\) and \(C'=CA^{-1}\); then \(C'\alpha '=C\alpha\). This proves only that the conditional mean is unchanged. Preserving the full GPFA marginal likelihood also requires transforming the latent prior covariance to \(A K A^\mathrm{T}\). Standard GPFA usually assumes independent factors that may have different temporal kernels; arbitrary rotation generally introduces between-factor covariance and leaves that model family. Sign flips, factor permutations, and paired scale changes are common ambiguities. More general rotational equivalence requires extra conditions such as identical kernels or an allowed correlated prior.

The GP prior supplies the temporal structure of \(\alpha\), while the observation model supplies the spatial relationship between r and \(\alpha\). Their roles cannot be reversed: C does not smooth time, and the kernel does not specify each neuron's loading. If \(\Sigma\) is diagonal, residual neurons are conditionally independent given the latent state. Strong remaining residual correlations may indicate too few factors K, a poor kernel, or an oversimplified noise model.
keyPoints: C is N×K and links latent space with neural activity space.
\(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data.
Conditional observation coordinates can be reparameterized; equivalence of the full GPFA also depends on the latent prior.

derivation.title: Shapes in the observation model and reparameterizing its conditional mean
derivation.setup: Check every vector shape, then prove that latent reparameterization leaves the conditional mean unchanged. This alone does not prove that the full GP prior or marginal likelihood is unchanged.

steps.title: List the shapes
steps.explanation: With N neurons and K factors, the matrix product must have N outputs.
steps.latex: C\in\mathbb R^{N\times K},\quad\boldsymbol\alpha_t\in\mathbb R^K,\quad\mathbf d\in\mathbb R^N

steps.title: Write the conditional mean
steps.explanation: The center of the observation Gaussian lies in activity space.

steps.title: Apply an invertible transformation
steps.explanation: Define the new latent coordinates as \(A\alpha\) and change the loading inversely.

steps.title: Verify unchanged predictions
steps.explanation: Multiplication cancels \(A^{-1}A\), so both coordinate systems give the same conditional mean. The transformed prior covariance must still be checked separately for the full model.

symbolNotes: N is the number of neurons and K is latent dimensionality, usually with \(K<N\).
\(\Sigma\) is an N×N covariance whose diagonal entries are residual variances. After transformation by A, a latent prior covariance generally no longer retains a factor-wise diagonal structure.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(C\alpha\) and d must share the units of r. If \(\alpha\) is dimensionless, entries of C have units of rate or count. \(\Sigma\) uses squared observation units.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(K=N\) and C is invertible, there is no dimensionality reduction. If all latent factors share an identical kernel, an orthogonal rotation can preserve the prior form; different kernels generally preclude arbitrary rotation.

workedExample.title: Reconstruct two neurons from one factor
workedExample.problem: Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates.
steps: A negative loading means that as the latent increases, the second neuron falls below baseline; it does not imply a negative firing rate.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Setting \(\alpha\) to 0 should recover the baseline \((10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\).

pitfalls: Treating a latent factor as a directly measured neuron.
Concluding from diagonal \(\Sigma\) that real neurons are independent; independence applies only to residuals conditional on the latent state.

modules.title: GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories
paragraphs: The squared-exponential kernel \(K(t,t')=\sigma s^{2}\) \(\exp[-(t-t')^{2}/(2\tau ^{2})]+\sigma n^{2}\delta tt'\) gives covariance between two times for one factor. \(\sigma s^{2}\) controls smooth signal variance, \(\tau\) controls the correlation-decay time, and \(\sigma n^{2}\) adds independent variability only in the same time bin. Because \(\alpha\) and loading C have a global scale ambiguity, impose \(\sigma n^{2}+\sigma s^{2}=1\) as a normalization convention. That constraint fixes scale; it is not a new biological law. Nor is this the only GP kernel: for rapid switching or oscillation, Matérn or periodic kernels may better match the hypothesis.

Fitting jointly estimates latent trajectories, loadings, baselines, noise, and kernel hyperparameters, commonly by marginal likelihood or an EM-like procedure. Increasing K always increases in-sample flexibility, so choose dimensionality with cross-validation, held-out likelihood, or reconstruction prediction. Training explained variance alone can mistake noise dimensions for meaningful factors.

Read a delayed-reach plot along its timeline. The interval after target onset but before the go cue is the preparatory epoch; movement begins only after go. Preparatory activity for different targets may approach different latent locations without producing obvious movement. After the cue, trajectories depart from those initial states along target-specific movement paths. The plot supports the idea that an initial condition influences later dynamics, but trajectories alone cannot exclude sustained common input.

Trial averaging clarifies preparatory trajectories but conceals single-trial onset jitter and variability. To claim that trajectory geometry predicts behavior, use the pre-go latent state to predict reaction time, directional error, or muscle activity on held-out trials. A post-go divergence may reflect alignment and condition averaging, so compare it with shuffled labels and alternative alignments.
keyPoints: \(\tau\) is a temporal correlation scale, not trial duration.
A kernel family is a modeling assumption that must be tested with held-out data.
Target, go, and movement events must delimit the epochs of a delayed-reach trajectory.

derivation.title: Two limits of the squared-exponential kernel
derivation.setup: Fix the time difference \(\Delta t\) and compare covariance when \(\tau\) is much larger or much smaller than that difference.

steps.title: Rewrite the time difference
steps.explanation: Let \(\Delta t=t-t'\) and first consider distinct time bins, for which the Kronecker delta is zero.

steps.title: Take the long-time-scale limit
steps.explanation: When \(\tau\) is much larger than \(|\Delta t|\), the exponent is close to zero.

steps.title: Take the short-time-scale limit
steps.explanation: For fixed nonzero \(\Delta t\), the exponent approaches negative infinity as \(\tau\) approaches zero.

steps.title: Add same-bin noise
steps.explanation: At \(t=t'\), signal variance and diagonal noise variance add.

symbolNotes: \(\sigma s^{2}\) and \(\sigma n^{2}\) have squared latent-amplitude units. The constraint \(\sigma n^{2}+\sigma s^{2}=1\) fixes this factor's arbitrary global scale.
\(\tau\) and t use the same time unit; \(\delta tt'\) is a discrete time-bin indicator.
derivation.unitsCheck: The numerator and denominator of the exponent both have units of time squared, so their ratio is dimensionless; K retains units of latent variance.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\tau \to \infty\), the factor is nearly constant within a finite window. As \(\tau \to 0\), between-bin covariance vanishes and the smooth prior degenerates.

workedExample.title: Compare correlation strength at two time lags
workedExample.problem: Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms.
steps: At \(\Delta t=100\), the exponent is -1/2 and \(K=e^{-1/2}\approx 0.607\).
At \(\Delta t=200\), the exponent is \(-4/2=-2\) and \(K=e^{-2}\approx 0.135\).
The second lag is twice as long, but covariance falls by more than a factor of four because distance is squared.
workedExample.result: The two values are approximately 0.607 and 0.135.
workedExample.sanityCheck: At \(\Delta t=0\) the value should be 1; the kernel decreases monotonically as \(|\Delta t|\) grows.

pitfalls: Mistaking \(\tau\) for the number K of latent factors.
Interpreting divergence after the go cue as recurrent causality without testing a sustained-input model.

modules.title: Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space
paragraphs: Write a locally linear readout as \(m=Ur\), where r is an N-dimensional neural state and m an M-dimensional motor command; U must therefore be M×N. Labeling U as N×M is incompatible with \(m=Ur\), so use M×N directly. Any nonzero r satisfying \(Ur=0\) lies in the null space of U; the neurons need not be silent. Preparatory activity can move the network along null directions without changing output in this approximation. After the go cue, the state enters potent directions and the readout becomes nonzero.

Rank–nullity gives dim Null\((U)=N-\operatorname{rank}(U)\). This simplifies to N-M only when U has full row \(\operatorname{rank} M\); if \(\operatorname{rank}(U)<M\), the null space is larger. When recording dimension greatly exceeds motor-output dimension, a large null space is theoretically possible. But recorded r samples only some neurons, and the true downstream map may be nonlinear, state-dependent, or delayed. The null space of a fitted U is therefore relative to a model, not an anatomically absolute no-output pathway.

Use the singular value decomposition of U to write r=rpotent+rnull. Row-space directions change output, while their orthogonal complement belongs to the null space. Test whether preparatory activity is output-null by fitting U on independent trials, measuring pre-go projections, and checking EMG or kinematics. Choosing a direction and reporting zero output on the same data is circular.

Output-null does not mean computation-null. Activity along a null direction can set a recurrent initial condition, suppress an erroneous movement, or prepare multiple candidates. The same neural vector may also affect unrecorded downstream populations. The course diagram is a linear framework that separates the existence of activity from the existence of current output; it does not justify calling null activity biologically functionless.
keyPoints: Null-space size is determined by input dimensionality and rank.
Output-null is a model statement relative to a specified readout U.

derivation.title: Rank–nullity and the potent/null decomposition
derivation.setup: For an M×N readout U, use linear algebra to show how a nonzero preparatory state can produce no output.

steps.title: Write the readout
steps.explanation: The output is a linear combination of the neural state.

steps.title: Define the null space
steps.explanation: All input vectors mapped to zero form a linear subspace.

steps.title: Compute its dimension
steps.explanation: Rank–nullity makes visible output directions and invisible input directions sum to N.

steps.title: Verify the decomposition
steps.explanation: If rnull is in the null space, it does not change the output determined by the potent component.

symbolNotes: M is the number of output coordinates, and N is the number of neural coordinates.
\(\operatorname{rank}(U)\) cannot exceed \(\min(M,N)\); all vectors must use the same centering convention.
derivation.unitsCheck: If r is in Hz and m in command units, U has units of command units/Hz; the zero vector carries the corresponding output units.
derivation.limitCheck: If U has full column rank and \(N\le M\), its null space contains only the zero vector. If N≫M, the null space has at least N-M dimensions.

workedExample.title: Compute an output-null vector
workedExample.problem: Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector.
steps: \(m=1\times 2+2\times (-1)=0\), so r is a nonzero null vector.
Adding the two vectors gives \((3,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), whose output remains \(3+2\times (-1)=1\).
workedExample.result: The null component changes the neural state without changing the original potent output of 1.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A null vector of U has zero dot product with the row vector (1,2), so the two are geometrically orthogonal.

pitfalls: Defining and testing the null space on the same training trials, thereby overfitting.

modules.title: Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment
paragraphs: A BMI decoder maps neural features to cursor velocity, position, or a discrete action. During open-loop calibration, the participant observes prescribed movement or attempts an action while the system fits a mapping offline. In closed loop, decoder output immediately changes visual feedback, so participant and decoder coadapt. Closed-loop performance is therefore not a passive measure of a fixed encoding; the brain, decoder, and feedback form a new dynamical system.

Suppose the observation on day d is \(r_{d}=C_{d}\alpha +d_{d}+\mathrm{noise}\). Different electrode samples change \(C_{d}\) while similar latent dynamics may persist. A cross-day method first estimates daily subspaces and then finds \(A_{d}\) to make their \(\alpha\) coordinates comparable; it finally applies \(\hat{v}=B\alpha\) in the aligned latent space. Stability here means that a transferable low-dimensional relationship exists, not that each neuron's loading is constant.

Alignment can manufacture false stability. If behavior labels from the current day rotate latent space and the decoder is then tested on that same day, the answer has leaked into the analysis. A strict evaluation uses calibration data alone to estimate \(A_{d}\) and B, tests on held-out blocks or future days, compares no alignment, random alignment, and a direct neuron-space decoder, and reports adaptation time and failure days.

These concepts form one closed loop: PCA/GPFA supplies a shared subspace, a linear readout supplies the behavioral map, closed-loop feedback changes the data distribution, and alignment handles coordinate drift. Every step has assumptions; 'stable latent structure' must not be expanded into permanent invariance of single-neuron representations.
keyPoints: A closed-loop BMI is a joint brain–decoder–feedback system.
Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity.
Holding out future days prevents behavior labels from leaking into the alignment result.

derivation.title: Mapping chain of a cross-day latent decoder
derivation.setup: Project each day's observation into a within-day latent space, align it to reference coordinates, and then decode.

steps.title: Write the daily observation
steps.explanation: Changes in electrode sampling appear in the daily loading and baseline.

steps.title: Align the coordinates
steps.explanation: Use \(A_{d}\) to map day d's latent coordinate into the reference latent space.

steps.title: Apply the shared decoder
steps.explanation: Use the same B for behavioral prediction in aligned coordinates.

steps.title: Define held-out error
steps.explanation: Compare true and predicted velocity on time bins used in neither alignment nor fitting.

symbolNotes: \(C_{d}\) is neurons×latents, \(A_{d}\) is latents×latents, and B is outputs×latents.
The number of neurons may vary across days, but aligned latent dimensionality must be constant.
derivation.unitsCheck: If velocity is in cm/s and the latent is dimensionless, B is in cm/s; squared error is in \(\mathrm{cm}^{2}/s^{2}\).
derivation.limitCheck: \(A_{d}=I\) means that no rotation is required. If latent subspaces do not overlap at all, linear alignment should not be expected to recover an accurate decoder.

workedExample.title: Swap the axes of a two-dimensional latent space
workedExample.problem: On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\).
steps: Use \(A=[[0,1],[1,0]]\) to swap the coordinates, giving \(\widetilde{\alpha }=(1,3)^\mathrm{T}\).
Without alignment, the result is \(2\times 3-1\times 1=5\), showing how a coordinate-convention change can seriously disrupt the decoder.
workedExample.result: The aligned prediction is -1; the unaligned prediction is 5.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A is a permutation matrix, so \(A^\mathrm{T} A=I\) and latent-vector length is unchanged.

pitfalls: Treating aligned latent stability as permanent stability of individual-neuron identity.
Using test-day behavior to choose an alignment and then reporting those same data as cross-day generalization.

figures.title: From population activity to closed-loop BMI
figures.alt: Population neural activity passes through GPFA latent inference, cross-day alignment, and a shared BMI decoder to produce cursor feedback, which then affects subsequent neural activity.
figures.caption: Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed.

synthesis: Directional tuning is a classic description of motor cortex, whereas the modern population view asks whether low-dimensional trajectories generate movement dynamics. GPFA embeds smooth latent factors into noisy neural activity with a Gaussian observation model and explicitly models temporal covariance. A preparatory state can vary within the null space of muscle readout U without causing movement. BMI decodes neural or latent state into device commands and uses feedback and cross-day latent alignment to improve stability.

Worked solution. Null(U) dimension=\(10-2=8\)；有大量 preparatory directions 不改变 2D output。 Check. \(Ur=0\) 不推出 \(r=0\)。

A K-dimensional trajectory in latent space is embedded by C into N-dimensional activity space. The column span of C is the shared-activity subspace allowed by the model, while \(\Sigma\) usually absorbs neuron-specific residuals. Shared variation does not require neuron pairs to have identical waveforms: positive and negative loadings allow one factor to produce different amplitudes and directions across cells.

Read a delayed-reach plot along its timeline. The interval after target onset but before the go cue is the preparatory epoch; movement begins only after go. questions.explanation: No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable. Output-null does not mean computation-null. Activity along a null direction can set a recurrent initial condition, suppress an erroneous movement, or prepare multiple candidates. The same neural vector may also affect unrecorded downstream populations. The course diagram is a linear framework that separates the existence of activity from the existence of current output; it does not justify calling null activity biologically functionless.

questions.explanation: The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes. A BMI decoder maps neural features to cursor velocity, position, or a discrete action. During open-loop calibration, the participant observes prescribed movement or attempts an action while the system fits a mapping offline. In closed loop, decoder output immediately changes visual feedback, so participant and decoder coadapt. Closed-loop performance is therefore not a passive measure of a fixed encoding; the brain, decoder, and feedback form a new dynamical system.
